claims.text: The dynamic mechanical response of solidified Co-free FeNiCrMn is governed by a temperature- and strain-rate-dependent balance between dislocation glide and deformation twinning.
High strain rates and low temperatures limit thermal activation in FeNiCrMn.
Limited thermal activation restricts dislocation climb and cross-slip.
Restricted climb and cross-slip lead to dislocation pile-ups and dense dislocation networks.
High-strain-rate, low-temperature deformation suppresses deformation twinning in FeNiCrMn.
Dislocation accumulation with minimal twinning increases yield strength.
Dislocation accumulation with minimal twinning reduces ductility.
Lower strain rates or higher temperatures promote deformation-twin formation in FeNiCrMn.
Deformation twins act as barriers to dislocation motion.
Increased deformation twinning enhances strain hardening and ductility retention.
High-temperature, low-strain-rate testing will produce lower yield strength and greater ductility than low-temperature, high-strain-rate testing.
Microscopy will reveal a shift from dislocation-dominant to twinning-dominant deformation as temperature increases or strain rate decreases.
The proposed mechanism applies to fully homogenized, defect-minimized, solidified equiatomic FeNiCrMn.
High levels of pre-existing cracks or voids may cause the proposed mechanism not to hold.
Microstructural states produced by alternative processing routes may fall outside the proposed mechanism's applicability.
Cobalt may cause related Co-containing high- or medium-entropy alloys to deform by different modes than Co-free FeNiCrMn.
Previous studies did not specifically isolate the interplay between dislocation glide and twinning in Co-free FeNiCrMn.
